claim: Cold exposure increases energy demands of thermogenesis which must be counterbalanced by increased energy intake to maintain energy homeostasis.
source: To maintain energy homeostasis during cold exposure, the increased energy demands of thermogenesis must be counterbalanced by increased energy intake.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that frames the biological context of the study.

claim: AgRP neuron activation occurs rapidly upon acute cold exposure.
source: We report that AgRP neuron activation occurs rapidly upon acute cold exposure, as do increases of both energy expenditure and energy intake, suggesting the mere perception of cold is sufficient to engage each of these responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data showing rapid increases in GCaMP signal in AgRP neurons upon cold exposure (Figure 4).

claim: Increases of both energy expenditure and energy intake occur rapidly upon acute cold exposure.
source: We report that AgRP neuron activation occurs rapidly upon acute cold exposure, as do increases of both energy expenditure and energy intake, suggesting the mere perception of cold is sufficient to engage each of these responses.
evidence: This is supported by metabolic cage data showing rapid increases in heat production and food intake within minutes of cold exposure (Figure 2).

claim: The mere perception of cold is sufficient to engage AgRP neuron activation, increased energy expenditure, and increased energy intake.
source: We report that AgRP neuron activation occurs rapidly upon acute cold exposure, as do increases of both energy expenditure and energy intake, suggesting the mere perception of cold is sufficient to engage each of these responses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rapidity of the responses observed in the study.

claim: Silencing of AgRP neurons selectively blocks the effect of cold exposure to increase food intake.
source: We further report that silencing of AgRP neurons selectively blocks the effect of cold exposure to increase food intake but has no effect on energy expenditure.
evidence: This is supported by chemogenetic inhibition experiments using hM4Di DREADD (Figure 5).

claim: Silencing of AgRP neurons has no effect on energy expenditure during cold exposure.
source: We further report that silencing of AgRP neurons selectively blocks the effect of cold exposure to increase food intake but has no effect on energy expenditure.
evidence: This is demonstrated by heat production measurements in DREADD experiments (Figure 5E, G, I).

claim: AgRP neurons play a physiologically important role in the hyperphagic response to cold exposure.
source: Together, these findings establish a physiologically important role for AgRP neurons in the hyperphagic response to cold exposure.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined findings of AgRP neuron activation and the effects of their inhibition.

claim: In homeothermic species, maintenance of euthermia in the face of a wide range of ambient temperatures is critical for survival.
source: In homeothermic species, maintenance of euthermia in the face of a wide range of ambient temperatures is critical for survival.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established biological knowledge.

claim: In small homeotherms, countering cold stress requires that adaptive adjustments of heat production occur rapidly and potently without depleting body fuel stored as fat.
source: In small homeotherms, countering cold stress requires not only that adaptive adjustments of heat production occur rapidly and potently, but also that they are achieved without depleting body fuel stored in the form of fat (Gordon, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gordon, 1993.

claim: When animals are housed in a cool environment, energy expenditure swiftly increases to generate the heat needed to maintain core body temperature.
source: Thus, when animals are housed in a cool environment, energy expenditure swiftly increases to generate the heat needed to maintain core body temperature (Cannon and Nedergaard, 2011) and, so long as a food is readily available, a compensatory hyperphagia prevents changes to body fat mass (Kaiyala et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cannon and Nedergaard, 2011.

claim: When food is readily available during cold exposure, a compensatory hyperphagia prevents changes to body fat mass.
source: Thus, when animals are housed in a cool environment, energy expenditure swiftly increases to generate the heat needed to maintain core body temperature (Cannon and Nedergaard, 2011) and, so long as a food is readily available, a compensatory hyperphagia prevents changes to body fat mass (Kaiyala et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kaiyala et al., 2012.

claim: Much is known regarding the neurocircuitry underlying cold-induced thermogenesis.
source: While much is known regarding the neurocircuitry underlying cold-induced thermogenesis (Madden and Morrison, 2019; Nakamura and Morrison, 2011; Tan and Knight, 2018), the origins of cold-induced hyperphagia remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Madden and Morrison, 2019; Nakamura and Morrison, 2011; Tan and Knight, 2018.

claim: The origins of cold-induced hyperphagia remain poorly understood.
source: While much is known regarding the neurocircuitry underlying cold-induced thermogenesis (Madden and Morrison, 2019; Nakamura and Morrison, 2011; Tan and Knight, 2018), the origins of cold-induced hyperphagia remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: During caloric restriction, the imposed negative energy balance and associated reduction of body fat stores drives adaptive homeostatic responses aimed at returning body fat stores to pre-intervention values.
source: During caloric restriction, for example, the imposed negative energy balance and the associated reduction of body fat stores drives adaptive homeostatic responses aimed at returning body fat stores to pre-intervention values.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about energy homeostasis.

claim: Reduced energy expenditure and increased hunger drive are major components of the adaptive response to caloric restriction.
source: Reduced energy expenditure and increased hunger drive are major components of this adaptive response, and both are thought to be primarily driven by humoral signals indicative of energy deficiency (e.g., reductions of leptin and insulin) (Schwartz et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schwartz et al., 2000.

claim: Reduced energy expenditure and increased hunger drive during caloric restriction are thought to be primarily driven by humoral signals indicative of energy deficiency (e.g., reductions of leptin and insulin).
source: Reduced energy expenditure and increased hunger drive are major components of this adaptive response, and both are thought to be primarily driven by humoral signals indicative of energy deficiency (e.g., reductions of leptin and insulin) (Schwartz et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schwartz et al., 2000.

claim: It has been reasonably assumed that the hyperphagic response to cold requires the same signals of energy deficiency as caloric restriction.
source: It has, therefore, been reasonably assumed that the hyperphagic response to cold requires the same signals of energy deficiency, and this hypothesis is supported by studies that have been conducted over time periods sufficient to induce hormonal changes (Bing et al., 1998; Hardie et al., 1996; Puerta et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bing et al., 1998; Hardie et al., 1996; Puerta et al., 2002.

claim: AgRP neurons are located in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (ARC).
source: Among central targets of these humoral feedback signals are neurons located in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (ARC) that express agouti-related peptide (AgRP) (Hahn et al., 1998) which, when activated, potently stimulate feeding (Aponte et al., 2011; Atasoy et al., 2012; Krashes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hahn et al., 1998.

claim: AgRP neurons, when activated, potently stimulate feeding.
source: Among central targets of these humoral feedback signals are neurons located in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (ARC) that express agouti-related peptide (AgRP) (Hahn et al., 1998) which, when activated, potently stimulate feeding (Aponte et al., 2011; Atasoy et al., 2012; Krashes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aponte et al., 2011; Atasoy et al., 2012; Krashes et al., 2011.

claim: AgRP neurons are regulated by humoral signals.
source: However, recent evidence suggests that, although AgRP neurons are regulated by humoral signals (Hahn et al., 1998; Schwartz et al., 2000), they may also be under feed-forward control (Chen and Knight, 2016; Lowell, 2019) such that they can be activated by neurocircuits that integrate sensory cues from the environment (Betley et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2015; Zimmer et al., 2019) and thereby avert a negative energy state.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hahn et al., 1998; Schwartz et al., 2000.

claim: AgRP neurons may also be under feed-forward control.
source: However, recent evidence suggests that, although AgRP neurons are regulated by humoral signals (Hahn et al., 1998; Schwartz et al., 2000), they may also be under feed-forward control (Chen and Knight, 2016; Lowell, 2019) such that they can be activated by neurocircuits that integrate sensory cues from the environment (Betley et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2015; Zimmer et al., 2019) and thereby avert a negative energy state.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen and Knight, 2016; Lowell, 2019.

claim: AgRP neurons can be activated by neurocircuits that integrate sensory cues from the environment and thereby avert a negative energy state.
source: However, recent evidence suggests that, although AgRP neurons are regulated by humoral signals (Hahn et al., 1998; Schwartz et al., 2000), they may also be under feed-forward control (Chen and Knight, 2016; Lowell, 2019) such that they can be activated by neurocircuits that integrate sensory cues from the environment (Betley et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2015; Zimmer et al., 2019) and thereby avert a negative energy state.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Betley et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2015; Zimmer et al., 2019.

claim: Chronic cold exposure at 14°C for 5 days does not significantly change core body temperature in mice compared to controls housed at 22°C.
source: Using a mild, chronic cold-exposure paradigm (14°C for 5 days) and comparing outcomes to mice housed at room temperature (22°C) (Figure 1A), we found that, as expected (Cannon and Nedergaard, 2004; Morrison et al., 2014), core body temperature did not change significantly relative to controls housed at room temperature (Figure 1B), presumably owing to an associated increase in heat production (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and citations to Cannon and Nedergaard, 2004; Morrison et al., 2014.

claim: Chronic cold exposure at 14°C for 5 days increases heat production in mice.
source: Using a mild, chronic cold-exposure paradigm (14°C for 5 days) and comparing outcomes to mice housed at room temperature (22°C) (Figure 1A), we found that, as expected (Cannon and Nedergaard, 2004; Morrison et al., 2014), core body temperature did not change significantly relative to controls housed at room temperature (Figure 1B), presumably owing to an associated increase in heat production (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The thermogenic response to chronic cold exposure at 14°C is accompanied by a proportionate increase in energy intake.
source: This thermogenic response was accompanied by a proportionate increase in energy intake (Kaiyala et al., 2015; Ravussin et al., 2014; Vallerand et al., 1986; Figure 1D), such that neither body weight nor body fat mass changed significantly over the course of the study (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and citations to Kaiyala et al., 2015; Ravussin et al., 2014; Vallerand et al., 1986.

claim: During chronic cold exposure at 14°C for 5 days, neither body weight nor body fat mass changed significantly.
source: This thermogenic response was accompanied by a proportionate increase in energy intake (Kaiyala et al., 2015; Ravussin et al., 2014; Vallerand et al., 1986; Figure 1D), such that neither body weight nor body fat mass changed significantly over the course of the study (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: During chronic cold exposure at 14°C for 5 days, neither respiratory quotient (RQ) nor ambulatory activity changed significantly.
source: Moreover, neither respiratory quotient (RQ) nor ambulatory activity changed significantly (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text but data is not shown.

claim: Chronic cold exposure at 14°C increases expression of orexigenic Agrp mRNA in the hypothalamus compared to controls housed at 22°C.
source: Despite our use of a mild cold-exposure paradigm, consistent with previous work using more severe cold-exposure paradigms (~4–5°C) (McCarthy et al., 1993; Tang et al., 2009), we found increased expression of orexigenic Agrp and Npy mRNA in animals housed at 14°C when compared to controls housed at room temperature, while expression of Pomc and Pmch remained unchanged (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1H and citations to McCarthy et al., 1993; Tang et al., 2009.

claim: Chronic cold exposure at 14°C increases expression of orexigenic Npy mRNA in the hypothalamus compared to controls housed at 22°C.
source: Despite our use of a mild cold-exposure paradigm, consistent with previous work using more severe cold-exposure paradigms (~4–5°C) (McCarthy et al., 1993; Tang et al., 2009), we found increased expression of orexigenic Agrp and Npy mRNA in animals housed at 14°C when compared to controls housed at room temperature, while expression of Pomc and Pmch remained unchanged (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1H and citations to McCarthy et al., 1993; Tang et al., 2009.

claim: Chronic cold exposure at 14°C does not change expression of Pomc mRNA in the hypothalamus compared to controls housed at 22°C.
source: Despite our use of a mild cold-exposure paradigm, consistent with previous work using more severe cold-exposure paradigms (~4–5°C) (McCarthy et al., 1993; Tang et al., 2009), we found increased expression of orexigenic Agrp and Npy mRNA in animals housed at 14°C when compared to controls housed at room temperature, while expression of Pomc and Pmch remained unchanged (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Chronic cold exposure at 14°C does not change expression of Pmch mRNA in the hypothalamus compared to controls housed at 22°C.
source: Despite our use of a mild cold-exposure paradigm, consistent with previous work using more severe cold-exposure paradigms (~4–5°C) (McCarthy et al., 1993; Tang et al., 2009), we found increased expression of orexigenic Agrp and Npy mRNA in animals housed at 14°C when compared to controls housed at room temperature, while expression of Pomc and Pmch remained unchanged (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Enhanced Agrp mRNA expression during cold exposure cannot be attributed to reductions of food intake or body fat stores.
source: Importantly, this evidence of enhanced Agrp mRNA expression cannot be attributed to reductions of either food intake or body fat stores, since the former was actually increased and the latter unchanged throughout the study period.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing increased food intake and unchanged body fat during cold exposure.

claim: In response to acute cold exposure at 14°C, increases in heat production occur rapidly and are detected within 5 minutes.
source: Our findings show that, in response to the sudden change in ambient temperature, increases in heat production occurred rapidly, such that the thermogenic response needed to maintain core temperature was detected within 5 min (Figure 2B) and remained elevated for the duration of the 24 hr study (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Heat production remains elevated for 24 hours during acute cold exposure at 14°C.
source: Our findings show that, in response to the sudden change in ambient temperature, increases in heat production occurred rapidly, such that the thermogenic response needed to maintain core temperature was detected within 5 min (Figure 2B) and remained elevated for the duration of the 24 hr study (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Upon acute cold exposure, the increase in food intake required to offset heightened thermogenic demand is equally swift as the thermogenic response.
source: Somewhat surprisingly, we also found that upon acute cold exposure, the increase in food intake required to offset heightened thermogenic demand was equally swift (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Neither RQ nor ambulatory activity is affected during acute cold exposure at 14°C.
source: By comparison, neither RQ nor ambulatory activity was affected during cold exposure, suggesting that they are unlikely to play an important role in the adaptive response to this challenge (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The initial increase in the rate of food consumption during acute cold exposure is maintained throughout both light and dark cycles.
source: Like the increase in heat production, the initial increase in the rate of food consumption was maintained throughout both light and dark cycles (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The rapid feeding response to cold exposure is unlikely to have resulted from any detectable depletion of body fat or associated circulating signal (e.g., leptin).
source: Based on the rapidity of this feeding response, we infer that it was unlikely to have resulted from any detectable depletion of body fat or associated circulating signal (e.g., leptin).
evidence: This is an inference based on the rapid time course of the feeding response.

claim: The perception of cold is sufficient to increase both food intake and energy expenditure rapidly and in parallel, independently of feedback signals.
source: We interpret these findings as favoring a model in which the perception of cold is sufficient to increase both food intake and energy expenditure rapidly and in parallel, independently of feedback signals that might be subsequently recruited.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the rapid and parallel increases in food intake and energy expenditure.

claim: Acute cold exposure at 14°C for 90 minutes increases the total number of Fos+ cells in the ARC compared to mice maintained at 22°C.
source: Although the total number of AgRP+ neurons was comparable in all mice tested (Figure 3C), relative to mice maintained at 22°C, we found that both the total number of Fos+ cells in the ARC (Figure 3D) and, specifically, the number of Fos+ AgRP neurons (Figure 3E and F) was increased within 90 min of cold-exposure onset.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Acute cold exposure at 14°C for 90 minutes increases the number of Fos+ AgRP neurons compared to mice maintained at 22°C.
source: Although the total number of AgRP+ neurons was comparable in all mice tested (Figure 3C), relative to mice maintained at 22°C, we found that both the total number of Fos+ cells in the ARC (Figure 3D) and, specifically, the number of Fos+ AgRP neurons (Figure 3E and F) was increased within 90 min of cold-exposure onset.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: The percentage of AgRP neurons that express Fos in response to cold exposure is approximately 25-30%.
source: However, while the percentage of AgRP neurons that expressed Fos in response to cold exposure (~25–30%) is similar to that previously reported in P10 mice separated from the warmth of the nest, dam, and littermates (Zimmer et al., 2019), it is less than that described following fasting (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on quantification of Fos+ AgRP neurons shown in Figure 3F and comparison to cited studies.

claim: Cold exposure increases Fos in the parabrachial nucleus (PBN).
source: As expected, we also found cold-induced increases in Fos in other thermoregulatory control centers including the parabrachial nucleus (PBN), preoptic area (POA) (Bratincsák and Palkovits, 2004; Geerling et al., 2016), dorsomedial hypothalamus (DMH) (Hunt et al., 2010), and rostral raphe pallidus (rRPa) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cold exposure increases Fos in the preoptic area (POA).
source: As expected, we also found cold-induced increases in Fos in other thermoregulatory control centers including the parabrachial nucleus (PBN), preoptic area (POA) (Bratincsák and Palkovits, 2004; Geerling et al., 2016), dorsomedial hypothalamus (DMH) (Hunt et al., 2010), and rostral raphe pallidus (rRPa) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations to Bratincsák and Palkovits, 2004; Geerling et al., 2016.

claim: Cold exposure increases Fos in the dorsomedial hypothalamus (DMH).
source: As expected, we also found cold-induced increases in Fos in other thermoregulatory control centers including the parabrachial nucleus (PBN), preoptic area (POA) (Bratincsák and Palkovits, 2004; Geerling et al., 2016), dorsomedial hypothalamus (DMH) (Hunt et al., 2010), and rostral raphe pallidus (rRPa) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to Hunt et al., 2010.

claim: Cold exposure increases Fos in the rostral raphe pallidus (rRPa).
source: As expected, we also found cold-induced increases in Fos in other thermoregulatory control centers including the parabrachial nucleus (PBN), preoptic area (POA) (Bratincsák and Palkovits, 2004; Geerling et al., 2016), dorsomedial hypothalamus (DMH) (Hunt et al., 2010), and rostral raphe pallidus (rRPa) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both the total number of Fos+ cells in the ARC and the number of Fos+ AgRP neurons are minimal in mice housed at 30°C.
source: Moreover, in contrast to both 14°C and 22°C, both the total number of Fos+ cells in the ARC and the number of Fos+ AgRP neurons were minimal in mice housed at 30°C (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Fos+ AgRP neuron number increases at temperatures below thermoneutrality.
source: Our finding that Fos+ AgRP neuron number increases at temperatures below thermoneutrality (Figure 3F) identifies ambient temperature as a potential physiological regulator of AgRP neuron activity.
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Ambient temperature is a potential physiological regulator of AgRP neuron activity.
source: Our finding that Fos+ AgRP neuron number increases at temperatures below thermoneutrality (Figure 3F) identifies ambient temperature as a potential physiological regulator of AgRP neuron activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temperature-dependent changes in Fos expression in AgRP neurons.

claim: Food presentation strongly and rapidly inhibits AgRP neuron activity in fasted mice.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Betley et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2015), we found that food presentation strongly and rapidly inhibited AgRP neuron activity, as indicated by a strong reduction in GCaMP signal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citations to Betley et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2015.

claim: When the temperature of the platform is rapidly reduced from 30°C to 14°C, an increase in GCaMP signal in AgRP neurons is detected within seconds.
source: Consistent with this prediction, we found that when the temperature of the platform was rapidly reduced from 30°C to 14°C (within 1 min) an increase in GCaMP signal was detected within seconds, consistent with an increase in AgRP neuron activity.
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: The increase in AgRP neuron activity induced by cooling from 30°C to 14°C is reversed by raising the temperature from 14°C back to 30°C.
source: Moreover, this effect was reversed by raising the temperature from 14°C back to 30°C (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Pretreatment injection of CNO in mice expressing the inhibitory DREADD in AgRP neurons attenuates cold-induced induction of Fos in AgRP neurons relative to saline-treated controls.
source: To further validate the ability of the inhibitory DREADD to reduce AgRP neuron responsiveness, we found that pretreatment injection of CNO in mice expressing the inhibitory DREADD in AgRP neurons attenuated cold-induced induction of Fos in AgRP neurons relative to saline-treated controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inhibition of AgRP neurons has little effect on food intake in mice housed at 30°C.
source: Consistent with this prediction, we found that whereas inhibition of AgRP neurons had little effect on food intake in mice housed at 30°C (Figure 5D), intake was strongly reduced in animals housed at 14°C, while intake was only modestly inhibited by CNO in mice housed at 22°C (Figure 5F and H).
evidence: This is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Inhibition of AgRP neurons strongly reduces food intake in mice housed at 14°C.
source: Consistent with this prediction, we found that whereas inhibition of AgRP neurons had little effect on food intake in mice housed at 30°C (Figure 5D), intake was strongly reduced in animals housed at 14°C, while intake was only modestly inhibited by CNO in mice housed at 22°C (Figure 5F and H).
evidence: This is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Inhibition of AgRP neurons modestly reduces food intake in mice housed at 22°C.
source: Consistent with this prediction, we found that whereas inhibition of AgRP neurons had little effect on food intake in mice housed at 30°C (Figure 5D), intake was strongly reduced in animals housed at 14°C, while intake was only modestly inhibited by CNO in mice housed at 22°C (Figure 5F and H).
evidence: This is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Room temperature (22°C) poses a thermal stress to mice.
source: The latter finding is consistent with room temperature posing a thermal stress to mice (Abreu-Vieira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Abreu-Vieira et al., 2015.

claim: Cold-induced increases of food intake and energy expenditure in AgRP-IRES-Cre mice expressing a control mCherry fluorophore do not differ following i.p. injection of CNO vs. saline.
source: Moreover, these responses cannot be explained by a nonspecific effect of CNO, as cold-induced increases of food intake and EE in AgRP-IRES-Cre mice expressing a control mCherry fluorophore did not differ following i.p. injection of CNO vs. saline (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by control data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The cold-induced increase in heat production is not affected by AgRP neuron inhibition.
source: The effect of AgRP neuron inhibition appears to be selective for energy intake, as the cold-induced increase in heat production was not affected (Figure 5E,G, and I).
evidence: This is supported by heat production data shown in Figure 5E, G, and I.

claim: There is no significant effect of AgRP neuron inhibition on RQ at any of the three ambient temperatures studied (30°C, 22°C, 14°C).
source: In addition, there was no significant effect of AgRP neuron inhibition on either RQ or ambulatory activity at any of the three ambient temperatures studied (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: There is no significant effect of AgRP neuron inhibition on ambulatory activity at any of the three ambient temperatures studied (30°C, 22°C, 14°C).
source: In addition, there was no significant effect of AgRP neuron inhibition on either RQ or ambulatory activity at any of the three ambient temperatures studied (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: AgRP neuron activation is required for cold-induced hyperphagia.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that AgRP neuron activation is required for cold-induced hyperphagia, and furthermore, distinct and separable neurocircuits underlie the feeding and thermogenic responses to cold.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the chemogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: Distinct and separable neurocircuits underlie the feeding and thermogenic responses to cold.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that AgRP neuron activation is required for cold-induced hyperphagia, and furthermore, distinct and separable neurocircuits underlie the feeding and thermogenic responses to cold.
evidence: This is an inference based on the selective effect of AgRP neuron inhibition on feeding but not thermogenesis.

claim: Some degree of cold stress (including housing at room temperature) is required for food intake to be reduced by chemogenetic AgRP neuron inhibition.
source: In addition, some degree of cold stress (including housing at room temperature) is required for food intake to be reduced by chemogenetic, AgRP neuron inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temperature-dependent effects of AgRP neuron inhibition on food intake.

claim: The tight coupling between thermoregulation and energy homeostasis enables animals to preserve both core body temperature and body fat mass across a wide range of ambient temperatures when food is available.
source: The tight coupling that exists between thermoregulation and energy homeostasis (Gordon, 1993; Kaiyala et al., 2015) enables animals to preserve both core body temperature and body fat mass across a wide range of ambient temperatures, so long as food is available (Kaiyala et al., 2015; Smith and Romsos, 1984; Thurlby and Trayhurn, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gordon, 1993; Kaiyala et al., 2015; Smith and Romsos, 1984; Thurlby and Trayhurn, 1979.

claim: Precise coupling exists between changes of energy expenditure and energy intake in response to changing requirements for heat production.
source: Fundamental to this process is the precise coupling between changes of energy expenditure and energy intake in response to changing requirements for heat production (Armitage et al., 1984; Kaiyala et al., 2015; Thurlby and Trayhurn, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Armitage et al., 1984; Kaiyala et al., 2015; Thurlby and Trayhurn, 1979.

claim: Cold-induced hyperphagia has been documented across many species, including humans.
source: While cold-induced hyperphagia has been documented across many species, including humans (Johnson and Kark, 1947), the mechanisms underlying this response have received little attention, especially when compared to the considerable literature describing how changes of thermogenesis are coupled with changes of ambient temperature (Madden and Morrison, 2019; Rezai-Zadeh and Münzberg, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Johnson and Kark, 1947.

claim: In normal mice, AgRP neurons are rapidly activated by cold exposure.
source: We report that in normal mice, AgRP neurons are rapidly activated by cold exposure and that intact cold-induced hyperphagia requires this activation, since increased food intake in this setting was blocked by acute chemogenetic AgRP neuron silencing.
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry and Fos data.

claim: Intact cold-induced hyperphagia requires AgRP neuron activation.
source: We report that in normal mice, AgRP neurons are rapidly activated by cold exposure and that intact cold-induced hyperphagia requires this activation, since increased food intake in this setting was blocked by acute chemogenetic AgRP neuron silencing.
evidence: This is supported by chemogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: The magnitude of food intake reduction induced by chemogenetic silencing of AgRP neurons varies inversely with increasing ambient temperature.
source: We also show that the magnitude of food intake reduction induced by chemogenetic silencing of these neurons varies inversely with increasing ambient temperature, such that the effect is more pronounced in colder environments relative to thermoneutral conditions in which AgRP neuron activity is lower.
evidence: This is supported by data showing temperature-dependent effects of AgRP neuron inhibition on food intake (Figure 5).

claim: Under experimental conditions in the absence of negative energy balance, the adaptive increase in food intake during acute cold exposure depends upon increases in AgRP neuron activity.
source: Taken together, we conclude that under our experimental conditions (e.g., in the absence of negative energy balance induced, for example, by caloric restriction), the adaptive increase in food intake during acute cold exposure depends upon increases in AgRP neuron activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined findings of the study.

claim: AgRP neurons are GABAergic neurons that co-express neuropeptide Y (NPY).
source: These GABAergic neurons co-express the potent orexigen neuropeptide Y (NPY) and are found exclusively in the ARC (Hahn et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hahn et al., 1998.

claim: AgRP neurons are found exclusively in the arcuate nucleus (ARC).
source: These GABAergic neurons co-express the potent orexigen neuropeptide Y (NPY) and are found exclusively in the ARC (Hahn et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hahn et al., 1998.

claim: POMC-neuron activation has the opposite effect on feeding compared to AgRP neuron activation.
source: An adjacent neuronal population expresses pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), and whereas AgRP neuron activation stimulates feeding, POMC-neuron activation has the opposite effect (Schwartz et al., 2000; Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schwartz et al., 2000; Xu et al., 2011.

claim: AgRP and POMC neurons are reciprocally regulated by leptin.
source: Furthermore, AgRP and POMC neurons are reciprocally regulated by leptin (Schwartz et al., 2000; Sohn et al., 2013) and other humoral signals, such that the effect of energy restriction to reduce body fat stores (and plasma leptin levels) causes both activation of AgRP neurons and inhibition of POMC neurons, a combined response that drives feeding until body fat stores and plasma leptin levels return to baseline values (Schwartz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schwartz et al., 2000; Sohn et al., 2013; Schwartz et al., 2017.

claim: Energy restriction reduces body fat stores and plasma leptin levels, causing activation of AgRP neurons and inhibition of POMC neurons, driving feeding until body fat stores and plasma leptin levels return to baseline.
source: Furthermore, AgRP and POMC neurons are reciprocally regulated by leptin (Schwartz et al., 2000; Sohn et al., 2013) and other humoral signals, such that the effect of energy restriction to reduce body fat stores (and plasma leptin levels) causes both activation of AgRP neurons and inhibition of POMC neurons, a combined response that drives feeding until body fat stores and plasma leptin levels return to baseline values (Schwartz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schwartz et al., 2017.

claim: The rapidity with which AgRP neurons are activated in response to cold exposure is unlikely to be explained by negative feedback control via humoral signals.
source: However, our data suggests that the rapidity with which AgRP neurons are activated in response to cold exposure is unlikely to be explained by this type of negative feedback control.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rapid time course of AgRP neuron activation.

claim: Humoral negative feedback signals could be recruited over time and play a role in sustained feeding responses to a cold challenge.
source: Nevertheless, humoral negative feedback signals could certainly be recruited over time and play a role in sustained feeding responses to a cold challenge, even if they are not relevant to the initial hyperphagic response.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms for sustained responses.

claim: AgRP neuron activity is influenced by 'feed-forward' signals that promote homeostasis by anticipating future changes to energy balance.
source: Recent work has established that in addition to negative feedback regulation by humoral signals relevant to body fuel stores, AgRP neuron activity is also influenced by 'feed-forward' signals that promote homeostasis by anticipating future changes to energy balance (Chen and Knight, 2016; Lowell, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen and Knight, 2016; Lowell, 2019.

claim: Cues from the environment that anticipate eating (e.g., the sight or smell of food) are feed-forward signals that influence AgRP neuron activity.
source: Among relevant feed-forward signals are cues from the environment that anticipate eating (e.g., the sight or smell of food), which are presumably communicated indirectly to AgRP neurons via cortical areas that process the relevant sensory input (Livneh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Livneh et al., 2017.

claim: Synaptic relays in the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus (PVN), dorsomedial nucleus (DMH), and pre-optic area (POA) may play a role in transmitting sensory information to AgRP neurons.
source: How this information is ultimately transmitted to AgRP neurons is unknown, but synaptic relays in the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus (PVN) (Krashes et al., 2014), dorsomedial nucleus (DMH) (Garfield et al., 2016), and pre-optic area (POA) may play a role.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Krashes et al., 2014; Garfield et al., 2016.

claim: AgRP neurons can be activated by sensory-related stimuli.
source: The key point is that although food intake driven by AgRP neuron activation is commonly associated with states of negative energy balance and/or falling leptin levels, these neurons can also be activated by sensory-related stimuli (Chen and Knight, 2016; Garfield et al., 2016; Krashes et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen and Knight, 2016; Garfield et al., 2016; Krashes et al., 2014.

claim: Exposure of P10 mice to a warm environment rapidly suppresses AgRP neuron activity.
source: Specifically, exposure of P10 mice to a warm environment rapidly suppresses AgRP neuron activity, whereas pup isolation (with reduced thermal insulation from the nest, dam, and littermates) increases AgRP neuron activity (Zimmer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zimmer et al., 2019.

claim: Pup isolation (with reduced thermal insulation from the nest, dam, and littermates) increases AgRP neuron activity in P10 mice.
source: Specifically, exposure of P10 mice to a warm environment rapidly suppresses AgRP neuron activity, whereas pup isolation (with reduced thermal insulation from the nest, dam, and littermates) increases AgRP neuron activity (Zimmer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zimmer et al., 2019.

claim: In neonatal mice, changes of AgRP neuron activity in response to temperature have no impact on food intake.
source: An important distinction from our work, however, is that in neonatal mice, these changes of AgRP neuron activity had no impact on food intake, consistent with previous work suggesting that control of food intake by AgRP neurons does not emerge until weaning (Gropp et al., 2005; Luquet et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gropp et al., 2005; Luquet et al., 2005.

claim: Control of food intake by AgRP neurons does not emerge until weaning.
source: An important distinction from our work, however, is that in neonatal mice, these changes of AgRP neuron activity had no impact on food intake, consistent with previous work suggesting that control of food intake by AgRP neurons does not emerge until weaning (Gropp et al., 2005; Luquet et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gropp et al., 2005; Luquet et al., 2005.

claim: In adult mice, the time course of increased AgRP neuron activity coincides with cold-induced increases of both energy expenditure and energy intake.
source: Another key finding reported herein is that in adult mice, the time course of increased AgRP neuron activity coincides with cold-induced increases of both energy expenditure and energy intake, and that each of these responses occur quite rapidly.
evidence: This is based on the combined findings from fiber photometry and metabolic measurements.

claim: The thermogenic response needed to maintain core body temperature during cold exposure is achieved within 5 minutes.
source: Thus, by commencing continuous monitoring upon placing mice in a pre-cooled cage (rather than waiting for the cage to gradually cool to the desired temperature), we were able to show that the thermogenic response needed to maintain core body temperature for the duration of the study was achieved within 5 min.
evidence: This is supported by heat production data in Figure 2B.

claim: Cold-induced hyperphagia has a similarly rapid onset as the thermogenic response, at least in mice studied during the mid-light cycle.
source: Even more impressive is that cold-induced hyperphagia had a similarly rapid onset, at least in mice studied during the mid-light cycle, when they are normally inactive and consume only a small percentage of their daily calories (Ellacott et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by food intake data in Figure 2D and citation to Ellacott et al., 2010.

claim: The rapidity and synchrony with which exposure to a cold environment activates AgRP neurons and engages feeding responses is consistent with control via a 'feed-forward' mechanism.
source: We interpret the rapidity and synchrony with which exposure to a cold environment activates AgRP neurons and engages feeding responses as being consistent with control via a 'feed-forward' mechanism, and future studies are warranted to test this hypothesis.
evidence: This is an interpretation and speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of AgRP neurons selectively blocks cold-induced hyperphagia without impacting cold-induced increases of energy expenditure, RQ or ambulatory activity.
source: Our findings further show that chemogenetic inhibition of AgRP neurons selectively blocks cold-induced hyperphagia without impacting cold-induced increases of energy expenditure, RQ or ambulatory activity, suggesting cold-induced AgRP neuron activation is required for the feeding, but not the thermogenic response to this challenge.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Cold-induced AgRP neuron activation is required for the feeding, but not the thermogenic response to cold exposure.
source: Our findings further show that chemogenetic inhibition of AgRP neurons selectively blocks cold-induced hyperphagia without impacting cold-induced increases of energy expenditure, RQ or ambulatory activity, suggesting cold-induced AgRP neuron activation is required for the feeding, but not the thermogenic response to this challenge.
evidence: This is an inference based on the selective effects of AgRP neuron inhibition.

claim: Reduced energy expenditure accompanies hyperphagia induced by chemogenetic activation of AgRP neurons.
source: Initially, these observations seem at odds with published evidence that reduced energy expenditure accompanies hyperphagia induced by chemogenetic activation of AgRP neurons (Cavalcanti-de-Albuquerque et al., 2019; Krashes et al., 2011), by fasting (Cahill et al., 1966), or by ghrelin administration (Tschöp et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cavalcanti-de-Albuquerque et al., 2019; Krashes et al., 2011.

claim: Reduced energy expenditure accompanies hyperphagia induced by fasting.
source: Initially, these observations seem at odds with published evidence that reduced energy expenditure accompanies hyperphagia induced by chemogenetic activation of AgRP neurons (Cavalcanti-de-Albuquerque et al., 2019; Krashes et al., 2011), by fasting (Cahill et al., 1966), or by ghrelin administration (Tschöp et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cahill et al., 1966.

claim: Reduced energy expenditure accompanies hyperphagia induced by ghrelin administration.
source: Initially, these observations seem at odds with published evidence that reduced energy expenditure accompanies hyperphagia induced by chemogenetic activation of AgRP neurons (Cavalcanti-de-Albuquerque et al., 2019; Krashes et al., 2011), by fasting (Cahill et al., 1966), or by ghrelin administration (Tschöp et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tschöp et al., 2000.

claim: During fasting, AgRP neurons play a pivotal role in both the drive to feed and the suppression of unnecessary fuel utilization, including thermogenesis.
source: This arrangement makes sense teleologically given that during fasting, the overarching need of fasted animals is to conserve fuel. In this setting, AgRP neurons are thought to play a pivotal role in both the drive to feed and the suppression of unnecessary fuel utilization, including thermogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge and teleological reasoning.

claim: Fasting-associated AgRP neuron activation inhibits the reproductive axis.
source: Adding further complexity is the fact that fasting-associated AgRP neuron activation also inhibits the reproductive axis (Padilla et al., 2017), whereas cold-exposed animals continue to reproduce (Barnett, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Padilla et al., 2017; Barnett, 1965.

claim: Cold-exposed animals continue to reproduce.
source: Adding further complexity is the fact that fasting-associated AgRP neuron activation also inhibits the reproductive axis (Padilla et al., 2017), whereas cold-exposed animals continue to reproduce (Barnett, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Barnett, 1965.

claim: Functionally distinct subsets of AgRP neurons may exist, with those involved in feeding drive in the cold being distinct from those that control energy expenditure or reproductive function.
source: One explanation for this seeming paradox is that functionally distinct subsets of AgRP neurons exist (Sternson and Atasoy, 2014), with those involved in feeding drive in the cold being distinct from those that control energy expenditure or reproductive function.
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Sternson and Atasoy, 2014.

claim: Cold exposure activates only a subset of AgRP neurons.
source: In support of this hypothesis, our Fos staining shows that cold exposure activates only a subset of AgRP neurons, whereas fasting and ghrelin administration each activate the majority of AgRP neurons (Andrews et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by Fos data in Figure 3 and citations to Andrews et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2012.

claim: Fasting activates the majority of AgRP neurons.
source: In support of this hypothesis, our Fos staining shows that cold exposure activates only a subset of AgRP neurons, whereas fasting and ghrelin administration each activate the majority of AgRP neurons (Andrews et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Andrews et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2012.

claim: Ghrelin administration activates the majority of AgRP neurons.
source: In support of this hypothesis, our Fos staining shows that cold exposure activates only a subset of AgRP neurons, whereas fasting and ghrelin administration each activate the majority of AgRP neurons (Andrews et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Andrews et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2012.

claim: The magnitude of cold-evoked calcium activity in AgRP neurons is less than what is observed following either fasting or ghrelin administration.
source: Similarly, in the context that our animals were fed ad libitum for our studies, and AgRP neuron responsiveness is known to be influenced by feeding state (Chen et al., 2015), we found that the magnitude of our cold-evoked calcium activity in AgRP neurons is less than what is observed following either fasting or ghrelin administration (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on comparison of fiber photometry data to published findings, supported by citation to Chen et al., 2015.

claim: Distinct subpopulations of AgRP neurons, projecting to different downstream brain areas, may mediate opposing effects on energy intake and energy expenditure.
source: These observations collectively support a model in which distinct subpopulations of AgRP neurons, projecting to different downstream brain areas, mediate opposing effects on energy intake and energy expenditure, and that cold exposure activates only the subset that stimulates feeding.
evidence: This is speculation based on the collective findings of the study.

claim: Cold exposure activates only the subset of AgRP neurons that stimulates feeding.
source: These observations collectively support a model in which distinct subpopulations of AgRP neurons, projecting to different downstream brain areas, mediate opposing effects on energy intake and energy expenditure, and that cold exposure activates only the subset that stimulates feeding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the selective effects observed in the study.

claim: The contribution made by AgRP neuron activation to food consumption is dependent on ambient temperature.
source: Further, we demonstrate that the contribution made by AgRP neuron activation to food consumption is dependent on ambient temperature, constituting a large fraction of intake during cold exposure while playing a lesser role in a thermoneutral environment.
evidence: This is based on the temperature-dependent effects of AgRP neuron inhibition on food intake.

claim: AgRP neuron activation constitutes a large fraction of food intake during cold exposure.
source: Further, we demonstrate that the contribution made by AgRP neuron activation to food consumption is dependent on ambient temperature, constituting a large fraction of intake during cold exposure while playing a lesser role in a thermoneutral environment.
evidence: This is based on the strong effect of AgRP neuron inhibition on food intake at 14°C.

claim: AgRP neuron activation plays a lesser role in food consumption in a thermoneutral environment.
source: Further, we demonstrate that the contribution made by AgRP neuron activation to food consumption is dependent on ambient temperature, constituting a large fraction of intake during cold exposure while playing a lesser role in a thermoneutral environment.
evidence: This is based on the minimal effect of AgRP neuron inhibition on food intake at 30°C.
